Section 6 of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 lays out the rules for how consent is required to process someone?s personal data. It makes consent the foundation for any data processing and gives individuals control over their information.
Key Points of Section 6: 
Consent 6(1)-Valid Consent Standards:Consent needs to be free, clear, informed, unconditional, and specific. This means people should actively agree to how their data is used, knowing exactly why it's being collected and for what purpose. It should never be vague or forced. Also, only the data necessary for that purpose should be collected.
6(2)-Invalid Consent:Any consent request that doesn?t follow the rules of this law or any other relevant laws is considered invalid.
6(3)-Clear and Accessible Consent:Requests for consent must be easy to understand, written in plain language, and available in English as well as the 22 languages listed in the Constitution. The consent request must also include contact details for a Data Protection Officer or someone authorized to answer questions.
6(4)-Right to Withdraw Consent:You can withdraw consent at any time, and the process of withdrawing should be as simple as giving it in the first place.
6(5)-Consequences of Withdrawal:If you withdraw your consent, you are responsible for the consequences. However, any data that was processed before you withdrew consent is still lawful.
6(6)-Ceasing Data Processing:When consent is withdrawn, the Data Fiduciary (the organization processing your data) must stop using your data as soon as possible, unless there?s another legal reason to continue processing it.
6(7)-Consent Managers:You can appoint a Consent Manager to handle and manage your consent on your behalf.
6(8)-Accountability of Consent Managers:Consent Managers are accountable to you, the individual, and must act according to your instructions and preferences.6(9)-Registering Consent Managers:Consent Managers must be registered with the Data Protection Board of India and meet the required conditions to operate.6(10)-Burden of Proof:The Data Fiduciary must prove that they?ve clearly informed you and obtained your valid consent before processing your data.

cmplst_long_description:
Sections 11 to 14 of India?s Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act, 2023) give people important rights over their personal data, making sure they have control and can see what's happening with it. These rights include:
The Right to Access (Sec 11)
The Right to Correct and Delete (Sec 12)
The Right to Grievance Redressal (Sec 13)
The Right to Nominate (Sec 14) someone to manage these rights on their behalf.
In other words, these sections empower individuals, giving them clear rights and control over their own personal data. Here's a breakdown of each right:
Section 11: Right to Access Information about Personal Data
You can ask if your data is being processed.
You can request a summary of your personal data and how it?s being used.
The organization handling your data must provide this info in an easy-to-understand way and without overcharging you.
Section 12: Right to Correct and Erase Personal Data
If any of your data is wrong or incomplete, you have the right to correct it.
You can also ask for your data to be erased (deleted) if it?s no longer needed or if you?ve withdrawn your consent.
Section 13: Right to Grievance Redressal
If there?s an issue with how your data is being handled, you can file a complaint.

Section 8 of India?s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 explains the responsibilities of Data Fiduciaries (the organizations or entities that control your personal data). It makes them accountable for ensuring your data is handled lawfully, securely, and accurately. This section covers both the actions of the Data Fiduciaries themselves and those of any Data Processors (third parties they may hire to handle data). There are also serious penalties for failing to comply.
Key Responsibilities under Section 8:
Overall Responsibility: Data Fiduciaries are responsible for following the rules of the Act, even if they delegate data processing to a third party (the Data Processor). They cannot avoid responsibility by passing the buck.
Data Processor Contracts: Data Processors can only use your data if there's a clear contract in place with the Data Fiduciary, and only for the specific purpose agreed upon.
Accuracy & Completeness: Data Fiduciaries must ensure that any personal data they collect is accurate, complete, and up to date. This is especially important if decisions are being made based on this data or if it will be shared with others.
Security Safeguards: Data Fiduciaries must take reasonable steps to protect your personal data from breaches. If a breach does occur, they must notify both the Data Protection Board and the affected individuals promptly.
Respecting Data Principal Rights: Data Fiduciaries must make it easy for you to exercise your rights, such as accessing your data, correcting it, having it erased, or filing a grievance if needed.
Reasonable Security: Data Fiduciaries must implement measures to secure your data. Failure to do so can result in hefty fines of up to ?250 crore.
Data Breach Notification: If there?s a data breach, the Data Fiduciary must notify the Data Protection Board and all affected individuals in a way that's prescribed by the rules.
Impact on Other Laws:
The DPDP Act aims to strike a balance between privacy and transparency. For example, it amends laws like the Right to Information (RTI) Act to ensure privacy rights are respected while still allowing access to public information, creating a more harmonized framework.
In simpler terms, Section 8 holds Data Fiduciaries accountable for making sure your personal data is processed securely, accurately, and in line with your rights. If they mess up, there are serious consequences.

Section 10 of India?s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 focuses on ?Significant Data Fiduciaries? (SDFs)?big players who handle large amounts of personal data. The government will identify these organizations based on factors like the volume of data, its sensitivity, and the impact they may have on public safety or people's rights. These SDFs face stricter rules to ensure they protect data better, including appointing a local Data Protection Officer (DPO), conducting regular audits, and enhancing security measures.
Key Points of Section 10:
What Makes an SDF?
The Central Government decides which organizations qualify as Significant Data Fiduciaries. This is based on how much data they handle, how sensitive that data is, and the potential risks to individuals' privacy or to public safety.
Data Protection Officer (DPO)
SDFs are required to appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) who is based in India. The DPO?s job is to serve as a point of contact for any issues or complaints and to report directly to the organization?s leadership.
Independent Audits
SDFs must bring in an independent auditor every year to assess whether they?re complying with the law and properly protecting personal data.
Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)
SDFs must conduct regular DPIAs to identify any risks to individuals' data rights. This helps them assess how they?re using data and if any changes need to be made to minimize harm.
Enhanced Security & Governance
These organizations need to implement stronger security measures and better governance practices. For example, they need to prevent harm from how they process data and ensure strict rules on how data is transferred across borders.
Purpose:
Section 10?s goal is to make sure that organizations that handle huge amounts of sensitive data are held to higher standards. This helps protect individuals? rights and makes sure that personal data is handled with extra care and transparency.
In simpler terms, Section 10 makes sure that the biggest and most influential data-handling companies are held to stricter rules, ensuring they have the systems in place to protect your personal information better.
